turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Why do my photos of the moon always come out as a blurry white dot?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: The moon is much brighter than the night sky, so the camera overexposes it. Lowering the exposure a lot usually brings back the detail.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm just using my phone.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Tap on the moon, then slide the brightness down until you see the craters. Zoom only as far as the phone's optical zoom goes.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Rest the phone on something solid, or use a small tripod. A two second timer stops your finger from shaking it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What does aperture actually mean? I keep reading it and nodding.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's the size of the opening in the lens that lets light in. A wide opening means more light and a blurrier background.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And the numbers, like f two?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Confusingly, smaller numbers mean a wider opening. So f two gives a soft background, and f eleven keeps everything sharp.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So for a portrait I'd want / the small number?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly. For a landscape where you want the whole scene sharp, go with a bigger number like f eight.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Got it. That makes way more sense now.

turns.text: Use a fast shutter speed, around one thousandth of a second, and burst mode. Then keep the sharpest shot.

turns.text: I'm an estate agent and I've got a tiny studio flat to list. How do I make it not look like a shoebox?

turns.text: Shoot from a corner, standing in a doorway if you can, with the camera at about chest height. That shows the most floor and makes the room feel deeper.

turns.text: She'd love to see them on the telly at Christmas.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then the app is plenty. Write the year and names in the file name as you go, while your mum is there to remember who's who.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh, she'll love that. She'll tell a story for every single one.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Bit embarrassing, but I want to try street photography and I'm scared of pointing my camera at strangers.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not embarrassing at all, almost everyone feels that. Would you be more comfortable starting without faces?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What do you mean?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Shadows, silhouettes, people walking away, hands, reflections in shop windows. You're still telling stories about the street, just more gently.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I like that. What if someone / notices me and gets annoyed?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Smile, show them the photo, and offer to delete it. Most people are curious more than angry.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And busy places are better, right? Like a market.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, at a market everyone's taking photos, so you blend in. A small camera or your phone draws less attention than a big lens.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. I'll try the Saturday market.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Give yourself a tiny goal, like twenty frames. Once that's done, anything else is a bonus.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I dropped my camera in the sand at the beach. It sounds crunchy when I zoom. Please help.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: First, don't zoom or turn it on and off any more. Grinding sand gets in deeper every time the lens moves.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oops. Okay, stopped.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Use a blower brush, not your breath, on the lens barrel and the buttons. Hold the camera facing down so the grains fall out rather than in.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I don't have a blower.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A soft clean makeup brush works for the outside. But if it still crunches after that, take it to a repair shop. Sand inside the zoom isn't a home job.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Will that cost a fortune?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A clean usually costs much less than a new lens. It's worth asking for a quote before you decide anything.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Lesson learned. Camera bag next time.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I get that blurry background in portraits? Mine always look flat.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Three things help. Get closer to your subject, move them further from the background, and use the widest aperture you have.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm only on a phone.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then portrait mode does it digitally. It works best when the person is about an arm's length or two away, with plenty of distance behind them.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Mine sometimes blurs the edges of her hair weirdly.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's the software guessing. A plain background and good light make the guess much easier. Busy leaves or fences behind her confuse it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So a park with a field behind, not trees.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly. Or open sky, or a long street. You can also reduce the blur strength after, a little blur looks more natural than a lot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We had our baby last week and I want some newborn photos, but I don't want to put her in weird poses.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Congratulations. Honestly, the simple ones are often the most loved. Her tiny hands, feet, yawns, her asleep on someone's chest.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's what I want. Natural stuff.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Shoot in the room with the biggest window, mid morning, flash off. Keep the room warm, sleeping babies are happiest when they're cosy.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I get my partner in them too?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Definitely. Close ups of her hand holding a finger, or her lying on your partner's arm, show how small she is.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We're exhausted though. / I don't want it to be a big project.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then don't make it one. Five minutes while she's asleep after a feed, a few days in a row, and you'll have a beautiful set.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's actually doable.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There are ducklings at the pond near me. They're so tiny and fast.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ducklings are such a treat to photograph. Can you get low, near the water?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Sort of, there's a little wooden jetty.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Lie on it if you can and shoot along the water. Eye level with the ducklings makes the photos feel like you're in their world.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My shots so far are just fuzzy brown blobs.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Use a fast shutter, at least a five hundredth of a second, and focus on the eye. If the eye is sharp, the rest can be a little soft.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if mum duck gets angry?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Keep your distance and use your zoom. If she starts hissing or herding them away, that's your cue to back off.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'll be good, promise.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My friend says all my photos are oversaturated. Rude, but is she right?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Possibly. A quick test is skin. If faces look orange or the grass looks like a cartoon, it's probably pushed too far.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, the grass is pretty neon.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Try lowering saturation and raising vibrance instead. Vibrance boosts dull colours but leaves the already strong ones alone.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Sounds like the same thing with a fancier name.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: They're close cousins, but vibrance protects skin tones. Edit one photo both ways and compare them side by side.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if I like neon?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then keep it. It's your style. Just make it a choice, not an accident, and maybe tone it down for portraits.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I paint in watercolour and I need to photograph my paintings for a gallery application. They always have a shiny glare.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Glare usually comes from light hitting the paper straight on. Are they framed under glass?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Two of them are, yes.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Take those out of the frames if you can. For all of them, put two lamps at forty five degrees on either side, and the camera dead centre.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Dead centre how?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: The lens pointing straight at the middle of the painting, parallel to it. If you tilt even slightly, the edges stop looking square.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And colour? The blues always come out purple.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Put a grey card or a white sheet in the first shot and set white balance from that. Then compare the photo to the real painting next to the screen.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's a lot more careful than I've been.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's worth it for a gallery. The jury only sees the photo, never the original.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It's been raining for a week and I'm getting cabin fever. Any photo ideas that don't need sunshine?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Rain is actually brilliant for photos. Puddle reflections, drops on a window with city lights behind, umbrellas from above.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Puddle reflections?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Put your phone right down near a puddle and flip the image later. Buildings and trees appear upside down in a little mirror world.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ha, I like that. What if I / really don't want to go out?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then try still life by a rainy window. A cup of tea, a book, the soft grey light makes everything moody.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Moody is my mood exactly.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Perfect match then. Turn off the room lights so only the window lights the scene, and you'll get lovely soft shadows.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Family reunion Sunday. Thirty people. Last time someone was blinking in every single group photo.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Thirty people means a blink in almost every frame, so the trick is taking lots. Use burst mode, or take at least ten in a row.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ten! They'll riot.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Tell them it's quick and keep talking while you shoot. Counting down to three and shooting on two catches people before they blink.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Sneaky. I like it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Also arrange them in rows on steps if there are any. Tall people at the back, kids at the front, and make sure you can see every face.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about me? I'm always missing.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Use a timer and a tripod, or hand the camera to a neighbour for the last few. You belong in the family photo too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I take nice photos of my food at restaurants without being that annoying person?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Keep it quick and quiet. Flash off, no standing on chairs, and one or two shots before you start eating.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Right, but the lighting in restaurants is always awful.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ask for a table by the window when you book. Daylight from the side makes food look amazing.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Huh, never thought of booking for the light.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then shoot from above for flat dishes like pizza, and at a low angle for tall things like burgers or layered cakes.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Do I / use the zoom?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Better to move the phone a bit closer than zoom in. And wipe the lens with a napkin first, it's often greasy from your fingers.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Everyone keeps saying shoot at golden hour. When is that exactly?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's roughly the first hour after sunrise and the last hour before sunset. The sun is low, so the light is warm and soft.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So it changes every day.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It does, with the seasons. A weather app usually shows sunset time, just count back about an hour.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Why is it better than midday?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Midday sun is overhead and harsh, so faces get dark eye sockets and strong shadows. Low sun wraps around people and makes long gentle shadows.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What's blue hour then? I heard that too.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Just after sunset, when the sky turns deep blue but there's still light. City lights against that blue look gorgeous.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, I'm going to have to start dinner later.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm going skiing and last year my camera battery died after like an hour.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Cold drains batteries fast. Bring at least one spare and keep it in an inside pocket, close to your body.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Inside pocket, got it. What about the camera itself?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It can stay outside in your bag. The tricky bit is coming indoors, warm air makes condensation on the cold camera.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh, that happened! It fogged up completely.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Put it in a sealed plastic bag before you go inside, and let it warm up slowly for half an hour before you open it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Any tips for the snow photos looking grey?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Snow fools the meter. Add a little exposure compensation, plus one or so, and the snow goes back to white.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We came back from three weeks in Portugal with two thousand photos. I want a photo book but I'm drowning.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Two thousand is normal. Start by picking only your favourites, quickly, with no second guessing. Aim for maybe a hundred.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: A hundred feels brutal.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Brutal is good here. A book with a hundred great photos is nicer than one with four hundred okay ones.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I decide though? / They all mean something.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ask whether each one tells a part of the story, like arriving, a meal, a view, a funny moment. Keep one strong photo per moment.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And then order them by date?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Date works, or by place. Mix in a few close details, like tiles or tickets, between the big views so the pages breathe.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Tiles! I took so many photos of tiles.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then they deserve a page of their own.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I want one of those silky waterfall photos. Mine just look like a normal waterfall.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That smooth water needs a slow shutter, usually half a second or longer, with the camera on a tripod.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I tried that and the whole thing went white.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Too much light is getting in. In daytime you need an ND filter, basically sunglasses for your lens, so you can keep the shutter open longer.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How dark a filter?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A six stop filter is a good all rounder for waterfalls. Or go on an overcast day, early, when there's less light anyway.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, overcast mornings, I can do that for free.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Use a two second timer so pressing the button doesn't shake anything, and keep the rocks sharp. The contrast with the smooth water is what makes it work.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I need a new profile photo for a job site. I hate how I look in pictures.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Lots of people do. The good news is a calm, friendly headshot is simple to get right. Do you have someone who can take it?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My flatmate, if I bribe her.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Great. Stand facing a window, about a metre from it, with a plain wall or some soft greenery behind you.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What do I / do with my face, though? I always look terrified.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Think of someone you like and say their name just before the photo. It gives a real half smile instead of a frozen one.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ha. Okay.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Have her hold the phone just above your eye level, and take loads. Pick the one where you look like yourself on a good day.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm seeing a band on Friday, standing room. Can I get decent photos from the crowd?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You can, with a few tricks. First check if the venue allows cameras, a lot only allow phones.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Just my phone then.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Turn off the flash, it's useless that far and annoys everyone. Tap on the singer to set focus and drag the exposure down so the stage lights don't blow out.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I film or take photos?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Take a few photos in the first couple of songs, when the lights are usually most dramatic, then put the phone away and enjoy it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's the real advice, isn't it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It is. A handful of good shots beats an hour of shaky video you'll never watch.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How big can I print a photo from my phone before it looks bad?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most modern phones are fine up to about A three for a wall, especially if you view it from a little distance.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I want it huge, over the sofa.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then it depends on the photo. Sharp, well lit shots in daylight hold up much better than dark ones or ones where you zoomed in.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It's a sunset at the lake. No zoom.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That should be fine pretty big. Order a small test print first to check the colours, phone screens often look brighter than paper.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Good idea. Canvas or paper?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Canvas hides a little softness and needs no frame, which is nice for a big sunset. Paper behind glass looks crisper but costs more to frame.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've got this little camera from my son for my birthday. How do I get the pictures onto my phone to send to the grandchildren?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Lovely present. Many cameras have an app that connects by wireless. Do you know the make of the camera?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It's written on the front, hang on. Yes, it's a Canon.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then there's a free Canon app for your phone. Install it, turn on wireless in the camera menu, and the app walks you through pairing them.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And after it's paired?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You'll see the camera's photos in the app. Tap the ones you like and save them, then they'll be in your phone's gallery to send as usual.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That sounds manageable. / My grandson said it was easy, but he says that about everything.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ha, they always do. Give it a try, and if it gets fiddly, a card reader that plugs into the phone is a simple backup.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm selling my car this week. How do I make the photos look good enough?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Wash it first, inside and out, it matters more than any camera trick. Then pick an empty spot with a plain background, like a car park on a Sunday.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Which angles do buyers want?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Front corner, back corner, both sides, the dashboard, the seats, the boot, and the tyres. And one clear shot of the mileage.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's a lot of photos.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It builds trust. Buyers skip ads with three blurry pictures. Shoot in the morning or on a cloudy day so the paint doesn't reflect everything.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There's a scratch on the back door.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Photograph it honestly. People feel better about a seller who shows the flaws, and it saves an argument when they come to look.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Fair enough.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've started a photo a day for a year. It's day forty and I'm already sick of it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Day forty is when most people hit the wall. What's making it feel like a chore?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I feel like I've photographed everything in my flat. Twice.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Try giving each week a theme. Only circles, only the colour yellow, only things from knee height. Limits make you see the same stuff differently.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Only things from knee height. That's ridiculous. I love it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: And allow yourself bad days. Some days the photo is your toothbrush and that's fine, the habit matters more than every picture.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My toothbrush is in like three already.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then it's practically a series. Look back at month one at the end of the year and you'll be amazed how much you've improved.

option_sets.lead_in: I want to get into photography, and I'm stuck choosing my first camera.
options: The first one is a used entry level camera with a kit lens, cheap and good for learning.
Then there's a new compact mirrorless camera that's small and light but costs a lot more.
Option three is skipping a camera and just buying a nicer phone with a great camera.
And the last one is an old film camera from a thrift store, which sounds fun but pricey to develop.
moshi_comment: For learning the basics, the used entry level camera is a smart, low risk start. The mirrorless camera is great if you'll carry it everywhere, since small cameras actually get used. A good phone is easiest, but you won't learn manual controls as well.
What do you want to photograph mostly? For travel, the light mirrorless is worth the extra cost. For learning on a budget, start with the used camera.

option_sets.lead_in: I'm planning a photo walk this weekend and can't pick where to go.
options: One option is the old downtown market early in the morning, when vendors are setting up.
Another is the botanical garden, which has a big flower show going on right now.
Or there's the harbor at sunset, with the boats and the bridge lit up.
moshi_comment: The harbor at sunset will give you the most dramatic light, especially with the bridge. The market is great for candid shots and street photography. The flower show is perfect for practicing close ups and color.
What kind of photos do you enjoy taking most, people, nature or landscapes? If it's people, the morning market is the best fit. You could even do the market and then the harbor later the same day.

option_sets.lead_in: My sister's wedding is in June and I've offered to sort the photographer. I'm overwhelmed.
options: There's a guy from her work who does it on weekends, cheap, but his website only has a few weddings on it.
A proper studio in town quoted us a lot, but they bring two shooters and a printed album.
Then a student from the art college who's really talented and hungry, though she's never done a wedding alone.
Or we could put disposable cameras on every table and let the guests do it.
moshi_comment: The studio is the safe bet if the budget allows, since two shooters means nothing gets missed. The art student could be a gem, but I'd want her paired with someone experienced. Disposable cameras are a fun extra, not a replacement.

Weddings only happen once, so I'd lean away from the coworker with only a few weddings to show. The student is the best value if you meet her first and see a full gallery. And the table cameras would make a sweet bonus either way.

option_sets.lead_in: I keep losing photos and I want a proper backup plan. Which of these makes sense?
options: I could buy an external hard drive and copy everything over every Sunday night.
There's a cloud storage plan that uploads straight from my phone automatically, monthly fee though.
My brother says get two drives and keep one at his place in case of a fire.
moshi_comment: The automatic cloud upload is the one you'll actually stick to, since it needs no effort. A single drive only works if you remember every Sunday. Your brother's idea is the gold standard, and pairs nicely with the cloud.
I'd combine them. Let the cloud catch your phone photos without thinking, and keep a drive at your brother's for the big archive. One drive on its own is a single point of failure.

option_sets.lead_in: I want to take a photography class this autumn but I can't decide which.
options: A ten week evening course at the community college, with homework and critique every week.
A weekend workshop in the mountains, two full days of shooting landscapes with a pro.
An online course I can do whenever, with videos and a forum, really cheap.
A street photography walk group that meets every Saturday morning, free, but no real teaching.
moshi_comment: If you want to actually improve, the evening course wins because weekly critique is gold. The mountain weekend is inspiring but short. The online one is fine if you're disciplined, which most of us aren't.

It depends what you're missing. Skills and feedback, take the college course. Motivation and company, the free Saturday group is great, and you could pair it with the cheap online course for the theory.

option_sets.lead_in: We need new photos for our bakery's menu board and I'm not sure how to do it.
options: I could just shoot them myself on my phone near the front window in the morning light.
My nephew has a nice camera and offered to do it for a cake.
There's a food photographer in the next town who charges a flat fee for half a day.
Or we skip photos and use hand drawn illustrations of the bread and pastries.
moshi_comment: For a menu board, your phone and that morning window light can honestly do the job, and you know the food best. Your nephew is a nice middle ground. The pro is worth it only if these photos go on your website and ads too.
Illustrations would give the bakery real character and never look dated. If you want photos, start with your phone, and only call the food photographer if the results look flat.
